props.title: The Ballad of Cable Hogue
props.initialSlug: Desert loner finds love and redemption at his waterhole

sections.content: **The Ballad of Cable Hogue** (1970) marks a fascinating shift in Sam Peckinpah's career, coming right after his ultraviolent masterpiece **The Wild Bunch** (1969). This gentler, more contemplative Western follows a prospector who discovers a water source in the desert and builds a successful rest stop. Jason Robards delivers a career-defining performance as Hogue, bringing humor and humanity to a character watching the Old West fade into modernity. The film brilliantly bridges traditional Western themes with the coming mechanical age.

sections.content: The film's treatment of progress and modernization connects it to other key Westerns of the era like **Monte Walsh** (1970) and **The Life and Times of Judge Roy Bean** (1972). These films collectively explore how the railroad, automobile, and industrial age transformed the American frontier. Peckinpah handles this theme with surprising gentleness and humor, contrasting sharply with the brutality of his other works.

The romantic subplot between Robards and Stella Stevens creates a unique tone for a Peckinpah film, more aligned with character studies like **McCabe & Mrs. Miller** (1971) than typical Westerns. The director's trademark slow-motion techniques appear but serve poetic rather than violent purposes, particularly in the bittersweet ending sequence. SUBHEAD: The End of the Western Golden Age

sections.content: **The Ballad of Cable Hogue** arrived as classical Westerns were giving way to more experimental takes like **Little Big Man** (1970) and **El Topo** (1970). These films questioned Western mythology while incorporating counterculture elements and surrealism. Peckinpah's film bridges this transition, maintaining traditional elements while embracing new storytelling approaches.
